d: What Uplink is, and where to start.
x: Uplink is one app for the people you talk to: your texts, your friends on Uplink, your circles with their chats, calls and files, and your Telegram, Signal and other chats, side by side. Messages between Uplink apps are sealed end to end, there are no ads, and the app is open source. Uplink is in alpha It works well enough to use every day, but things still change quickly and some features are marked Coming soon . If you're testing it, start with Join the alpha , and tell us anything odd in the Alpha testers circle. Start here Install the app Android, Mac, Windows or Linux, and what to say yes to. The first time you open it The welcome, and whether Uplink takes over your texts. Your account Create one, keep your recovery words safe, sign in elsewhere. Circles A group with its own spaces: chat, voice, files and texts. The Marketplace Plugins, built in and from other developers. Your texts on a computer Pair the Mac, Windows or Linux app with your phone. Build a plugin Make your own, try it in Developer mode, and submit it. Developer docs How the app is built, both APIs, and a Postman collection. Finding your way around Everything starts from the rail down the left of the screen, the same on every page, as Discord and Slack have. At its head is Messages , your conversations. Under it are your circles , each as its picture: tap one to open it, and a halo in its colour marks the one that's open. A dot beside a circle means something's unread; a red number means someone mentioned you. The circled plus under them starts a new circle or joins one by its link. At the foot: New (start a conversation, a group, a space or a circle), Contacts , Archive , the Marketplace (plugins, as a store) and Settings . Hold a pointer over any of them for its name. Right-click one, or press and hold it on a phone, for its menu: a circle's has its settings and members, Archive's marks everything in it read, and the Marketplace's and Settings' jump to a section. BC NO Messages Codes Circles MC Maya Chen See you at 7! 4:12 2 D Dad 📷 Picture Yesterday BC Book Club Sam: Chapter 9 tonight? Mon The conversations list, with the rail down its left: Messages, your circles, then New, Contacts, Archive, Marketplace and Settings. Prefer a dock? The rail is how you move around the app from 0.9.36. Settings › Developer › Navigation can put back a dock along the foot instead: One dock is the same on every page, and Changing dock is the earlier way, where a circle had a dock of its own. At the top of Messages are three tabs: Messages (texts and chats), Codes (sign-in codes, kept out of the way) and Circles . A few words we use Word What it means Circle A group of people with a sidebar of spaces, a bit like a small server. You can be in as many as you like. Space A room in a circle (or on its own): chat and voice, text only, files, or an SMS space for people without the app. Friend Someone you talk to over Uplink rather than by text: added by their username, or by their number once you've sealed your texts together. Connections Your other chat accounts linked into Uplink: Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix. Routes How messages travel between Uplink apps: over the relay, or by text. Plugin An extra you add from the Marketplace : for yourself, or, built in, for everyone in a circle. On which devices Android phone : everything, including your texts (SMS and picture messages). Mac, Windows and Linux : friends, circles, calls, files and your other chats on their own, and your texts when paired with your Android phone. iPhone Coming soon : friends, circles and calls. Apple doesn't let apps send or read texts outside the EU, so no texts.

d: Recovery words, your password, the account address, and being the same you on every device.
x: You don't need any of this to use Uplink. It's here for when you want to know what your account is, where it's kept, and what happens when you sign in somewhere else. One identity, on every device Your account is a key that's yours alone, made from your 12 recovery words. Every device you sign in on becomes that same you: your friends see one person, a circle sees one member, and everything sent to you reaches each of your devices. Your username (like @alex ) is how friends find you. It points at your key. Your password unlocks a sealed backup of your key, so you can sign in with a username and password instead of the words. Your 12 recovery words are the key. They work without the password, and nothing else can replace them. The account address The address that starts with 0x , shown when your account is made and in Settings › Me › Account , is your account's public name. It's the same in any wallet app that takes your 12 words, because it's made from them in the same standard way. Uplink doesn't use it for money; it's simply the one name your account has everywhere. Sharing it is safe; sharing your words is not. What the server keeps The relay server at gogho.st keeps your username and a backup of your key, sealed with your password, which is stretched on your device first. The server can't open it. It never sees your recovery words, your password, or your messages. Kept by the server Never sent to it Your username, and the key it points to Your recovery words Your sealed backup (only your password opens it) Your password Your verified number, if you verify one, to text you codes What you write, to anyone A computer paired with your phone A Mac or PC paired with your phone used to be someone of its own. Now it can be the same you: in Settings › Me › Account on the computer, tap Become the same you as your phone , or sign in to the account your phone is in. Account Become the same you as your phone Keeps who you are now, the same you as your phone Sign in to your Uplink account The account your phone is in On a paired computer. If you lose a device Sign in on another device, with your username and password or your words. In Settings › Me › Account › Signed in on these devices , remove the lost one. It's signed out the next time it connects: a lost iPhone, computer without a phone or browser then deletes everything of your account from itself, and a lost Android phone forgets your recovery words and its keys. If you think someone has your words, make a new account and tell your friends; the words can't be changed.

d: What a plugin of your own can do, what it is made of, and how it reaches the Marketplace.
x: A plugin of your own sorts texts the way you'd like them sorted: bills in a tab of their own with the amount on the row, a parcel's tracking number a press away, receipts marked read as they come. It's one file you write by hand that says what to look for in a text and what to do with it. You try it on your own device in Developer mode, then send it to the Marketplace, where it's reviewed before anyone else can add it. What a plugin can do Tag texts by their words : "your bill is ready", "amount due $45.20", a tracking number. A tag can keep what it found, like the amount. Give texts a tab of their own beside Messages and Codes, or a kind in the list's filter that people show or hide. Draw its texts' rows : a value large on the row (the amount, a tracking number), a short caption, a face with a letter and a colour, and a button at the row's end. Add buttons : lines in a conversation's menu in the list, a button in a conversation's header, lines in a message's menu. A button can say something, copy words to the clipboard, write a reply for you to send, mark the conversation read, move it to one of the plugin's tabs or back to Messages, or open the plugin's own web page. Act as texts come : mark texts in its own tabs and kinds as read, or take their notification away, but only behind a switch in its settings that starts off. Have settings of its own : switches, choices, and words the person types (more words for bills, say), shown on its page in the Marketplace. What it can't do It can't reach the internet, and it isn't code: nothing in it runs. It's a description the app follows. A button you press can open its one web page in your browser, and that's all. It never sees your contacts' texts, group texts, texts sent with Uplink's encryption, your own messages, chats on other networks (Telegram, Signal and the rest), or circles and spaces. It never acts on a text with a sign-in code in it. It can tag one, but never sort it into a tab, mark it read or silence it. It can't change the words of a message, or who a conversation is from: a row always keeps the conversation's own name. It's for you alone, on one device. Plugins from other developers can't be turned on for a whole circle yet. One file: ghost-plugin/1 A plugin is one file, id .ghostplugin , of JSON in the ghost-plugin/1 format: its name and description, its icon, what it may do, its settings, and its rules. It finds words in a text with phrases like amount due {amount} , never with code or regular expressions, so no plugin can hang the app, and one that's slow is paused. Every field is on The plugin file . { "format": "ghost-plugin/1", "id": "mybills", "version": "1.0.0", "name": "My bills", "tagline": "Bills in a tab of their own", "description": "Texts that say a bill is ready go to a Bills tab, with the amount on the row.", "symbol": "calculator", "hue": "amber", "shelf": "organise", "labels": ["bills"], "permissions": ["sort"], "rules": { "tags": [{"tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "detail": {"from": "token"}}], "sections": [{"key": "bills", "label": "Bills", "icon": "calculator", "kind": "tab", "takes": {"tagged": ["bill"]}, "row": {"value": "{tag:bill}"}}] } } That's a whole plugin, as small as one can be: Developer mode loads it as it is. To submit it, it also needs an icon, your username and a help address ( the whole Bills file has them). Where it runs An Android phone : everything, as your texts come. A computer paired with an Android phone : it sorts the phone's texts there too, once it's added on the computer (plugins are added on each device on its own). Marking read and silencing as texts come happen on the phone only. A Mac or Windows PC on its own has no texts, so a plugin does nothing there. iPhone : plugins from other developers aren't on iPhone at all, because of the App Store's rules for apps that add other developers' features. Developer mode can still load your own there, to try it with Try it . From an idea to the Marketplace Write it Start from one of the examples below and change it, or write one from nothing with The plugin file beside you. Any text editor will do. Try it in Developer mode Load it in Settings › Developer › Plugins in development from a file, a link or the clipboard, then try it on a text without waiting for one to come. Change it, press Reload , try it again. Your first plugin walks through it. Submit it Marketplace › Submit a plugin : the plugin, its icon, description and tags, a screenshot or two, and a note for the reviewer. Submit it to the Marketplace . Review A person at Uplink reads the whole file, tries it, and approves it, asks for changes or turns it down. Marketplace › My submissions shows where it stands, and the app tells you when that changes. Listed Approved, it's in Discover for everyone with the Reviewed mark, under your username. People see what it can do before they add it, and can report it from its page. The examples' ids, bills and parcels , load in Developer mode like any other, but can't be submitted ( id_example : "That's the example's id: give your plugin an id of its own."), so nobody takes the id every reader of these pages starts with. The icon Not needed in Developer mode: without one, the plugin's tile draws its symbol on its hue. Submitting needs one, and the submission form makes it for you from any picture you choose or paste (256 pixels a side, smaller if it must be), so you only need what follows to put one in the file yourself. A PNG, square, 64 to 512 pixels a side, holding only the chunks IHDR , PLTE , tRNS , sRGB , gAMA , pHYs , IDAT and IEND , with nothing after IEND : so no animation, no text, no EXIF and no colour profile ( bad_icon otherwise). In base64, the standard alphabet with = padding and no spaces or line breaks: at most 48,000 characters, and at most 36,000 bytes once decoded. It's drawn over the plugin's hue, filling its tile. Transparent parts show the hue, so a white glyph on transparency looks like a built-in plugin's tile. To make the base64 on a Mac: base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n' In PowerShell on Windows: [Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('icon.png')) Words in a plugin Every string in a plugin, its phrases included, keeps these rules ( bad_text , or phrase_bad_text for a phrase): No space at its start or end. One line. Only the description , whatsNew and settings' hint s may have line breaks, and only the plain one ( \n ). Nothing invisible: no control characters, zero-width spaces or joiners, direction marks or overrides, soft hyphens, private-use characters (one draws a company's logo on some systems), tag characters, or blank-looking letters that make a name look empty. Lengths are counted as JavaScript and Dart count them, in UTF-16 code units: most letters are one, and an emoji is often two. A name, and a section's label, can't be a built-in plugin's or one of their tabs' and kinds', nor have uplink , ghost or gogho in it ( name_reserved ). They're compared with look-alikes folded first, so "Сodes" with a Cyrillic С, or "Ｃｏｄｅｓ" in wide letters, is still Codes. x: A plugin's rules say what it does: tags it gives texts by their words, sections (tabs and kinds) that take tagged texts, actions (buttons and menu lines) and incoming rules for texts as they come. Any of them can say when it applies with a condition. The examples here are from Bills and Parcels . "rules": { "tags": [], // up to 32 tag rules "sections": [], // up to 4 tabs and kinds "actions": [], // up to 12 buttons and menu lines "incoming": [] // up to 8 rules for texts as they come } (JSON has no comments: they're only to say what each is.) Each part may be left out, but a plugin needs at least one tag rule or one section ( empty_pack ). Conditions A condition, a rule's when or a section's takes , is an object whose keys are all optional. Every one given must hold. Key Holds when from The sender is one of these, 1 to 50 of them, each 3 to 64 characters. A number is compared by its digits alone, so +1 (555) 010-0100 and 15550100100 are the same; a name a company texts from is compared in any case. An entry with no digit or letter in it, such as (-) , matches nobody. tagged The text has every one of these tags, 1 to 8 of the plugin's own. untagged It has none of these, 1 to 8. setting A switch's key alone: that switch is on (its default until the person changes it). Or {"key": "level", "is": "loose"} : that choice is loose (its default until changed); for a switch, "is" is "on" or "off" . section Actions only: the conversation is in this section of the plugin's own, or "main" for Messages. Never true in a message's menu, which isn't in a section. Anywhere else it's section_condition . A plugin with an incoming rule can't use from anywhere ( from_with_incoming ): nobody can judge a rule that marks read or silences texts from numbers they don't know. Nor can a plugin with a link button ( bad_link_when ): a tag given by sender, a tab that takes by sender or that tab's row would offer the link for those numbers alone, and pressing it would tell the page which numbers wrote. In a tag rule, tagged and untagged see only the tags given by the rules before it, so naming a tag no earlier rule gives is unknown_tag . Everywhere else, a tag no rule gives is unknown_tag , and a section the plugin doesn't have is unknown_section . There's no condition on groups: a plugin never sees one. Tags A tag rule gives a text a tag when its words match. Several rules may give the same tag: they're different ways to get it. { "tag": "bill", "any": ["your bill is ready", "amount due {amount}"], "atLeast": 1, "none": ["unsubscribe"], "wordsFrom": "extra", "when": {"untagged": ["paid"]}, "detail": {"from": "token"} } Field What it is tag The tag it gives. Required. any 0 to 30 phrases , at least atLeast of which must match. atLeast 1 to 5, and 1 if left out. At most the number of any phrases, unless it has wordsFrom too. all 1 to 8 phrases that must all match. none 1 to 20 phrases none of which may match. wordsFrom A words setting's key: the words the person typed there join any , each a plain phrase ( their own words ). when A condition. detail What the tag keeps: words of your own (1 to 200 characters); {"from": "token"} , what a phrase's first token found; or {"from": "match"} , the whole of what a phrase matched. Nothing if left out. A rule needs something to start it: any , all , wordsFrom , or a when with from or tagged ( tag_rule_no_trigger ). How a text's tags are worked out For each text the plugin sees, its tag rules run in the order they're written, each one like this: If its when doesn't hold, with the tags given so far, the rule is passed over. Its phrases are its any , then the person's words from wordsFrom . If it has either, it counts how many of them match the text; fewer than atLeast , and it's passed over. A rule whose only phrases are the person's words does nothing until they type some. If it has all and one of them doesn't match, or none and one of them does, it's passed over. Its detail: your own words, if that's what it says; for {"from": "token"} , going through its phrases in order, what the first token found in the first phrase that has a token and matches; for {"from": "match"} , the whole match of the first phrase that matches. Trimmed, cut to 200 characters, and nothing where it's empty. The text gets the tag if it hasn't got it yet. If it has it already with no detail, and this rule found one, the detail is kept. Whenever one of the plugin's settings changes, every conversation's tags are worked out again. An example of wordsFrom Bills has a words setting, More words for bills , and its first rule says "wordsFrom": "extra" . Someone who types council tax, water rates there gets "Your council tax is due next week." in their Bills tab, though none of Bills' own phrases match it. A tab is a tab of its own in the list, beside Messages and Codes; a kind is a line in the list's filter, which people show or hide in Messages as they do the built-in kinds. Field What it is key 1 to 12 lower-case letters, unique in the plugin. label 1 to 24 characters: its tab's words, or its line in the filter. Not a built-in's ( name_reserved ). icon An icon name . kind "tab" or "filter" . leavesMain Tabs only, true if left out: its conversations leave Messages for the tab. false keeps them in Messages too. On a kind it's leaves_main_on_filter . takes A condition with tagged or from ( takes_nothing otherwise), and no section . Required. row How its conversations' rows look ( below ). Every section needs the sort permission. A plugin's kinds start shown, and the person hides one in the filter as they would any kind. Built-in plugins sort first Built-in plugins' tabs and kinds are asked first, then plugins from other developers in the order they were added, each one's sections in the order written: the first that takes a conversation has it. So a plugin never takes what Codes or the spam filter takes, nor what a kind of Kinds of text takes. Kinds of text is on from the start, and its Payment reminders and Deliveries tracking take most bill and parcel texts before any other plugin is asked. Your plugin still tags them, but its tab gets them only where the person switches that kind off, in Marketplace › Kinds of text . An action is offered only where its when holds and the plugin sees the text, and a copy only where its placeholders can be filled. Its section condition reads the section the conversation is in. x: A plugin finds words in a text with phrases : plain words, like your bill is ready , with tokens where something varies, like amount due {amount} . There are no regular expressions and no code. The app turns each phrase into a search of its own making, with every repeat in it bounded, so a phrase can't run away with a phone however long or strange the text it reads. A phrase A phrase is 1 to 120 characters on one line, keeping the rules for words in a plugin . Read from left to right: { starts a token , which runs to the next } : a name, then optionally :N or :N-M . {digits:6} is {digits:6-6} , exactly six digits. {{ is a plain { , and }} a plain } . A run of spaces is one gap, which matches any run of space in the text: one space, several, a line break. Everything else is matched as it is: letters in any case, and every other character as itself. A . is a full stop, never "any character". The tokens Token Matches For example {digits:N-M} A run of N to M digits, not part of a longer run. 1 to 24, and 1-24 if you give no numbers. your code is {digits:4-8} finds 123456 in "Your code is 123456.", and nothing in "Your code is 1234567890". {number} A number: 1,234, 1.234,5, 98765 or 12.5. The whole run of digits, dots and commas it sits on, or nothing: 192.168.1.1 is no number. order {number} finds 1,234 in "Order 1,234 shipped". {amount} A number with a currency sign or code before or after it: $45.20, 45,00 EUR, £30. The signs are $, €, £, ¥ and ₹; the codes USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, in any case. amount due {amount} finds $1,234.56 in "Amount due $1,234.56 by Friday", and nothing in "Amount due 45 by Friday". {code:N-M} A whole word of N to M letters and digits with at least one digit in it. 4 to 24, and 4-10 if you give no numbers. code {code:4-8} finds AB12CD in "Use code AB12CD to sign in", and nothing in "Use code ABCDEF to sign in". {word} One word: letters, digits, ' and - . {word} delivery finds Acme in "Your Acme delivery is near". {words:N-M} N to M words of anything but spaces, between two plain parts of the phrase. 0 to 4, and 1-3 if you give no numbers. your {words:0-3} has shipped finds "new blue parcel" in "Your new blue parcel has shipped!" {url} A web address starting http:// , https:// or www. . track {url} finds https://example.com/t/123 in "track https://example.com/t/123 now". {email} An email address. from {email} finds bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk in "Reply from bob.smith+x@mail.example.co.uk." {phone} A phone number of 7 to 15 digits, with spaces, brackets, dots or dashes among them. The whole run it sits on, or nothing: two numbers with only a space between them read as one run. {phone} finds +1 (555) 010-0100 in "Call +1 (555) 010-0100 today". {date} A date: 12/03/2026, 2026-11-20, March 5th, 5 jan. Months are in English. on {date} finds March 5th in "Your appointment on March 5th at 3pm". {time} A time: 3pm, 10:30 a.m., 14:05. at {time} finds 10:30 a.m. in "See you at 10:30 a.m. sharp". The rules a phrase keeps A phrase that breaks one of these doesn't load, and says which at its place in the file ( rules.tags[0].any[2] ). They're checked in this order, and the first one broken is the problem given. Punctuation may touch one: #{digits:4-10} and code:{code} are fine. bill{digits:4} phrase_token_touches_word {words} needs a space on each side, so it can't be first or last. {words:1-2} bill phrase_words_edge {url} must be followed by a space or the end of the phrase. {url}. phrase_url_followed At most 4 tokens, and only one {words} and one {url} among them. a {digits} b {digits} c {digits} d {digits} e {digits} phrase_too_many_tokens A phrase with no token needs at least two letters or digits. a phrase_too_short Besides those: a token the app doesn't know, numbers it can't take, a { with no } or a } on its own is phrase_bad_token ( {digits:0} , {digits:9-4} , {foo} , code {code:3} , go {words:5} , x {word:2} y , bill } ). An empty phrase, one over 120 characters, one with a space at its start or end, a line break or an invisible character is phrase_bad_text . How a phrase matches Whole words. A phrase that starts or ends with a letter or digit matches only whole words there: bill finds "bill" in "Your bill is ready", but nothing in "Your billing statement". Any case. Letters match in either case, accented ones too: your appt finds "YOUR APPT", and café finds "CAFÉ". Curly quotes and dashes. Before matching, the text and the phrase both have curly quotes made straight, dashes made - and odd spaces made plain ones, so don't forget finds "Don’t forget" written with a curly apostrophe. The first 2,000 characters of a text are read, and the rest isn't. The anchor. A phrase's longest run of plain letters and digits (a to z, 0 to 9), at least three long, is its anchor: the first, where two are as long. The phrase is only tried on a text that has its anchor in it, in any case, which is how hundreds of phrases stay quick. your code is {digits:4-8} 's anchor is your , and tracking no. {code:8-24} 's is tracking . A phrase with no such run, like {phone} , at {time} or café , is anchorless : it's tried on every text, so a plugin may have only 8. What a match gives A match gives two things: the whole of what the phrase matched, and what its first token found. A tag rule's detail keeps one of them for its tag, for a row or a copy button to show: {"from": "token"} : what the first token found. amount due: {amount} on "Amount due: 45,00 EUR." keeps 45,00 EUR. {"from": "match"} : the whole match. d: What gets a plugin listed, what keeps one out, and how reports and withdrawals work.
x: Plugins in the Marketplace read people's texts, so they're held to more than working. These are what review looks for. Sending a plugin means saying, in the form, "I made this plugin, and it follows the Marketplace guidelines". What gets a plugin listed It does what it says. Its name, short line and description say what it does, and it does that and nothing else. Its phrases are precise. They match the texts it's for and not others. A phrase that's one short word, or a word like "your", catches far too much: Try the samples shows what yours catches, and a dinner plan or a sign-in code should come out untouched. What marks texts read or silences them is behind a setting , off until the person switches it on. The file format makes sure of that, so it's only a matter of saying clearly, in the setting's words, what it does. Its help link or email works , and reaches you. Its screenshots show it as it is , with made-up texts. Its words are plain. A description that says what it does, with no web addresses in it and no promises it can't keep. What keeps one out Another company's name, logo or marks anywhere in a plugin: its name, short line, description, tabs and kinds, faces, buttons, settings, icon or screenshots; or in your username or help address. A plugin that sorts a bank's texts can say "bank", not the bank's name. Looking like Uplink or a built-in plugin : its name, icon, colours or words. Screenshots showing real people's messages, names or numbers , yours included. Links to anything but your own pages. A plugin's one link is for its help or its own site. Anything hateful, sexual or harassing , in any of its words or pictures. Replies that aren't plain and polite. A button that writes a reply writes words the person sends as their own. Reports Anyone who has a plugin, or sees it in the Marketplace, can report it from its page with Report this plugin : why (it's misleading; it's harmful or abusive; it's spam; it asks too much of their texts; it doesn't work; or something else) and a few words. Their username goes with it only if they switch on Send my username with it . Every report is read, by a person, as soon as we can, and the harmful ones first. A report can lead to a plugin being taken off the Marketplace, a version being withdrawn, or its developer being blocked. Unlisting, withdrawing and blocking Unlisting takes a plugin off the Marketplace: nobody new can add it, and people who have it keep it. You can do it yourself from My submissions; review can do it too, and then only review can list it again. Withdrawing is for a version that should never have been approved. Every device that has it switches it off and says so ("Trips was withdrawn from the Marketplace and is off."), and its page gives the reviewer's reason: "Withdrawn from the Marketplace: … It's off, and does nothing until you remove it." It offers only Remove , and Update where a newer version is approved. The developer sees Withdrawn by review , with the same reason. An approved update doesn't withdraw the version before it unless review chooses to, so nobody's plugin stops working because they haven't updated yet. Blocking a developer stops them submitting ("This account can't submit plugins."), and may take their plugins off the Marketplace too.

d: What is sealed, what the server sees, blocking, reporting, and signing out.
x: Uplink is built so the people running its server can't read what you say. There are no ads, and the app is open source, so anyone can check. What's sealed end to end What Sealed end to end? Messages between friends, and in groups of friends Yes, with forward secrecy Circles and spaces: chat, files, polls Yes, with a key the circle's members share Calls Yes, between the people in them: through Uplink's relay, or directly where the relay can't be reached, still sealed Your texts with one person, with encryption on Yes Ordinary texts and picture messages No: they go through your carrier, as all texts do Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp and Matrix chats As those networks seal them; they go between your device and the network, not through Uplink What the server sees Which installs talk to each other, and when, as any server passing messages would. Your username, and your account backup sealed with your password (which it never sees). Your verified number, if you verify one, to text you codes. It's shown to nobody unless you choose. Never: what you write, your files, your recovery words or your password. On your device Spam filtering, sorting, translation, summaries, captions and transcripts all happen on your device. Your texts stay in your phone's own store. Plugins say on their pages what they can see. Plugins from other developers are reviewed before they're listed. They never see your contacts' texts, group texts, encrypted texts or your own (and nothing at all while Uplink can't read your contacts, since it couldn't tell them from strangers), and they have no way to send anything over the internet: a button you press can open the plugin's page in your browser or copy words to your clipboard. The Marketplace is fetched from our server, which sees your device's address and which plugins you add, and keeps no record of either. A report sends the plugin, what you chose and wrote, and your username only if you say so. A plugin you submit is listed with your username, help address and screenshots. Blocking and archiving Block someone from a conversation's menu or their card; an Uplink person when you report them. Settings › Blocked lists everyone you've blocked, Telegram and Signal people too, and unblocks them. Archive a conversation by swiping it left. Settings › Archived (or Archive in the rail) has them; a new message brings one back. Forward secrecy Messages between friends, and the copies your devices send each other, are sealed so that they stay safe even if your recovery words, your password or your account backup leak later. Each of your devices makes a fresh key every day and deletes it about two weeks later. A message is sealed with a one-off key that is thrown away as soon as it's sent. Someone who saved the scrambled traffic can't open it afterwards, even with your recovery words. What it doesn't cover: the messages saved on your devices (whoever has your unlocked phone can read your history), who you talk to and when, and data texts. It also doesn't cover circles yet, or messages to someone who has a device on an older version of Uplink; those use the earlier sealing. If your recovery words leak, someone could pretend to be you from then on. Compare safety numbers if something seems off, and make a new account if your words were exposed. Reporting Report someone who sends spam, harasses you, pretends to be someone else or shares something illegal. Uplink doesn't scan anyone's messages: a report is how the team hears about it. A message: press and hold it in a chat with a friend, a group of friends, or a space, and choose Report . A person: open their card (tap their name or picture) and choose Report . Choose why, add a note if you like, and press Send report . Reporting a person also offers to block them: you stop being friends, and their friend requests and messages to you are dropped. Unblock them in Settings › Blocked . Our server can't read your chats, so a message report takes the message and up to five messages either side of it with it, because you choose to hand them over. The report is sealed on your device so that only the Uplink reviewer can open it: the server keeps it without being able to read it. Your username goes with it, so the reviewer can tell reports apart; the person you report isn't told who reported them. Settings › Reports you've made lists what you've reported from this device: who, why and when, never the messages. In circles A circle's messages are sealed with a key everyone in it has. Forward secrecy doesn't cover circles yet. Removing someone stops their app joining, but it doesn't change that key, so an old or altered app that kept it could still read what's said. For anything a removed person mustn't read, make a new circle. See Removing someone . Leaving Settings › Me › Remove everything about me unlinks every account and your number, and clears your watch list, on the phone and on the server. Settings › Me › Account › Sign out of this device signs the device out. On an iPhone or a computer without a phone it offers to delete everything of your account from it too, and a browser always does; an Android phone, or a computer linked to one, keeps its texts and conversations. d: How messages travel between Uplink apps: the relay, your own relay, texts, and testing them.
x: Between Uplink apps (friends, groups, encrypted texts), messages can travel more than one way. Settings › Routes shows the ways your phone reaches others, tried from the top: one that fails or gets no answer gives way to the next. Routes Routes Relay server Through a server on the internet. The server sees who talks to whom, never what is said. SMS As data texts over the phone network. Each counts as a text on your plan. The ways this phone reaches another, tried from the top. People you can reach MC Maya Chen Last by the relay server Press one to send a test and see which route carries it. Settings › Routes on the phone. The relay server Uplink's relay server (at gogho.st) passes sealed packets between apps: friends, circles, spaces and calls' setup. It can't read them; it sees only which installs are talking, as any server would. It's also where your username, your sealed account backup and a circle's sealed files are kept. Your own relay server Anyone can run the relay on a server of their own and use it in place of ours. Under Settings › Routes › Relay server , type its address ( relay.example.com is enough) and press Check it and use it . Nothing changes unless an Uplink relay answers there; when one does, the app tells you what moving means and switches only when you say so. The section always shows which relay is in use, and Go back to Uplink's relay switches back in one press. Running the server itself is on Run your own relay . Routes Relay server Your own relay: relay.example.com In use · connected Passes messages to other relays A friend on another relay, added as @name@their.relay, is reached through this one. Go back to Uplink's relay gogho.st, where everyone else is. Another relay server's address relay.example.com Check it and use it Nothing changes unless an Uplink relay answers there. Relays can pass messages to each other. Add a friend on another relay as @name@their.relay. Everything else is still kept on each relay apart. Settings › Routes on a relay of your own. Friends on another relay Relays can pass sealed messages to each other, so a friend doesn't have to use the same relay as you. Each of you goes on using your own, and the two relays hand each other what you write. Neither can read it. To add someone on another relay, open Contacts , tap Add a friend , and type their username with their relay after it: @maya@relay.example . Nobody is asked while you type: their relay is asked when you tap Add , through yours where it talks to theirs. They are kept, and shown, under that name, and their card says which relay they are on. Add a friend Their username @maya@relay.example M maya@relay.example On relay.example: Add asks that relay Add Adding someone on another relay. Whether a relay talks to others is up to whoever runs it, and it is off until they switch it on. Settings › Routes says which yours is: Passes messages to other relays , or Doesn't pass messages to other relays . It takes both relays: where yours doesn't, the app asks their relay itself (as nobody: not as you), tells you the request can't be passed on yet, and sends it again by itself for two weeks. Where yours says theirs won't take messages from it, that is the answer. What crosses relays, and what doesn't yet Crosses: friend requests and everything friends write each other, where both relays talk. Messages for someone who is away wait at their own relay. Doesn't yet: calls, circles and spaces (each is a room on one relay), and who's online. The app says so instead of ringing a friend on another relay, keeps their ring as a missed call, and leaves them out of circles and spaces. Kept on each relay apart: usernames ( @maya on yours and @maya@relay.example can be two people), your account and its backup, invite words and Files spaces. Add-me links made on a relay of your own name it, so whoever opens one is asked for on that relay, from whichever relay they use. A link that names none is someone on gogho.st. Invite links to a circle or a space made on a relay of your own name it too. Opened by someone on another relay, the app says which relay the circle is on and which to use first, instead of joining it where nobody is. Your username follows you: moved to another relay, the app claims it there too where it is free, and your profile asks for one where someone else has it. Back on the relay you left, you have the one you had. Still works with anyone: texts (SMS), including encrypted ones. The Marketplace always comes from gogho.st. Off on a relay of your own unless you set them up: calls through a TURN server, verifying numbers by text, linking Discord, X or Telegram. Closed iPhones can't be woken by your relay. Someone on an older version of the app can't be reached from another relay: the app tells you they need a newer one. Where it is their relay that doesn't pass messages on, it says that instead. So a relay of your own suits a group that moves together, for its circles, spaces and calls, and its people can still be friends with people elsewhere. How to run one (Docker, or systemd behind Caddy or nginx, with coturn for calls) is on its own page: Run your own relay . The sample files are in the repository, in relay/deploy/ . Direct A second way between Uplink apps, tried after the relay server: straight from one device to another. The relay stays first, because it is fast and keeps a message for someone who is away. The direct route is the way through when the relay can't carry something, for instance when it can't be reached, and the way your app checks what the relay says (below). It starts off. Switch it on under Settings › Routes on an Android phone or a computer (the Mac, Windows or Linux); it isn't in the iPhone app or the browser yet. Until you switch it on, none of it runs on your device. Before you do, Settings says what it means. Your device links only with your own other devices and with your friends' devices. They are told where it is in sealed messages; nobody else is, and nothing is put in any public directory. What crosses a direct link is sealed exactly as it is through the relay. Routes Routes Relay server Through a server on the internet. The server sees who talks to whom, never what is said. Direct Off. Straight between your devices and your friends', for when the relay server can't carry something. Their devices learn this device's network address, and nobody else is told it. SMS As data texts over the phone network. Each counts as a text on your plan. The ways this phone reaches another, tried from the top. Direct Only through link helpers Friends' devices then see the link helper's address and not this device's. It is slower. A link helper sees which devices link and how much they send, never who they are or what is said. Settings › Routes, before Direct is switched on. Routes Direct Knows 3 friends' devices And 1 other device of your own. Linked to 1 device now 1 straight. Only through link helpers Friends' devices then see the link helper's address and not this device's. It is slower. A link helper sees which devices link and how much they send, never who they are or what is said. Settings › Routes, with Direct switched on. Who counts as a friend: only someone you and they both said yes to, as a friend by username or by number. People you share a group with, and people who have only asked, are never linked with or told anything. What a friend's device learns: your device's network address, as with any direct connection, and on a phone only while you're using the app. Switch on Only through link helpers and friends are told at once, and from then see the helper's address instead; links are slower then. You can switch it on before you switch Direct on, so that no friend's device ever sees your address. It is off unless you switch it on, because where the relay names no link helper, nothing would link at all. Link helpers are servers that help two devices find each other across networks, and pass their sealed packets along where no straight path can be made. The relay you use names them. Where it names none (a relay of your own that hasn't been given one), Settings says so: devices behind most home routers can't link then, and direct links work only between devices that can reach each other as they are, such as two on the same network. On a phone the direct network runs only for something of your own: a message you send, or the relay being unreachable while you use the app. It stops two minutes after, whatever a friend's device does, so it doesn't wear the battery down; with the app put away nothing of it keeps the phone awake. On a computer it stays up while the route is on. Invisible: while you've chosen to be shown as Invisible, your device makes no direct links with friends' devices, since a link would show it is there. Your own devices still link with each other. Off: switch Direct off under Routes and every link is closed at once, nothing is linked, and nobody is told where your device is. What it knew of your friends' devices stays, for when you switch it on again. If it can't start on your device, Settings › Routes says why under Direct , and every other route works as before. Local network A third way between Uplink apps: straight between devices on the same Wi-Fi or wired network, with no server and no internet at all. It comes after the relay server and Direct, as the way through when neither can carry something, and by itself it keeps you talking where there is a network and no internet: a cabin, a plane's Wi-Fi with nothing behind it, an office whose line is down. It starts off. Switch it on under Settings › Routes on an Android phone or a computer (the Mac, Windows or Linux); it isn't in the iPhone app or the browser. The first time, a Mac asks whether Uplink may find devices on your local network, and Windows asks whether it may be reached on private networks: say yes, or the route stays down and Settings says so. Straight between your devices and your friends' while they are on the same Wi-Fi or wired network as this one, with no server and no internet. SMS As data texts over the phone network. Each counts as a text on your plan. The ways this phone reaches another, tried from the top. Linked to 2 devices now Maya Chen at 192.168.1.20. Your other devices at 192.168.1.14. Anyone else on the network sees that a copy of the app is at this address, never who you are. Settings › Routes, with the local network switched on. How devices find each other: every few seconds your device says it is here to the whole network, in a way only your own devices and your friends' can recognise: a mark for each of them, made from the key the two of you already seal messages with, good for ten minutes and for the one address it is said from, and mixed with noise that looks the same. It names nobody. Anyone else on the network can tell that some copy of Uplink is at that address, and roughly how many people it could have at most (under 8, under 16, under 32 and so on): not who you are, not who your friends are, not how many you have. Someone who says your device's words again from their own address is recognised by nobody. Who it links with: your own other devices and your friends' devices, as Direct does. Never people you only share a group with, and never someone who has only asked to be a friend. Both devices need the route switched on and the app open. What a link is: each device proves to the other that it holds your shared key before anything is sent, and everything after is sealed for that link, on top of the sealing every message already has. d: Run the relay on a server of your own: what you give up, Docker or a single program, TLS, TURN for calls, and its settings.
x: Uplink's relay is one small program. Anyone can run it on a server of their own and point their app at it under Settings › Routes › Relay server . This page is for whoever runs that server: what you get and what you give up, how to run it with Docker or as a single program, calls through your own TURN server, a link helper, and how to check it and keep it updated. Read this first The app talks to one relay at a time for everything that goes through a relay. Moving to your own changes who you can reach and what still works. The next section says how, plainly. It suits a group that moves together, such as a family or a team. What you get, and what you don't Relays can pass sealed packets to each other, so friends can be on different relays. That is the keeper's choice on each relay, and it is off unless switched on ( below ). Everything else a relay keeps is still that relay's own. What On a relay of your own Friends by username: requests, messages, reactions, edits, read marks Yes , between people on your relay. With people on another relay too, where both relays talk to each other: add them as @maya@their.relay . Circles and spaces Only between people on the same relay. A link made on your relay names it at its end ( …@relay.example.com ): opened by someone on another relay, the app says which relay the circle is on instead of joining an empty room there, and a browser guest opening a space's link is connected to the relay it names. Calls Only between people on the same relay: a call is a room on one relay. The app says so instead of ringing a friend on another relay. Calls that can't go straight between two devices need your own TURN server . Who is online, away, last seen Not shown for a friend on another relay. Your account (username and password, the sealed backup) Kept on the relay you made it on. Signing in on a new device works only with that device on the same relay, and the sign-in screen says which relay it asks. An app moved to a relay that doesn't hold its account keeps everything and offers List this device again , which puts the account on that relay from the device. Your username Kept on each relay apart. @maya on yours and @maya@relay.example can be two people. When the app moves to another relay your username is claimed there too where it is free; where someone else holds it, your profile asks you to choose one for that relay. The one on the relay you left is yours again when you go back. Add-me links ( gogho.st/add/… ) A link made on your relay names it after the key ( #KEY@relay.example.com ). Whoever opens it is asked for on that relay, from whichever relay they use; a link that names none is someone on gogho.st. The link's key makes sure it is only ever the person who shared it. Circle invite words ( gogho.st/c/… ) Kept on each relay apart. A word made on your relay works typed into Join a circle by people on your relay; the gogho.st page only knows gogho.st's words. Files spaces Kept on your relay's disk, for people on your relay. Texts (SMS), encrypted ones included Unchanged. They go over the phone network, not through any relay. The Marketplace Always Uplink's, read from gogho.st whatever relay you use. Submitting a plugin needs a username claimed on gogho.st, so it doesn't work from your relay. Verifying your number; linking Discord, X, Telegram Off unless you set up your own Twilio Verify service and your own apps with those networks. Waking a closed iPhone Not possible. It needs Apple's push key for the app, which only the app's publisher holds. An iPhone gets what was held for it the next time the app is opened. Share feedback Goes to your relay where you set up a board for it; where you didn't, the app sends it to gogho.st instead, since it is about the app. A computer paired to the phone Messages go through the phone, so through your relay, and the computer's own connection for spaces goes to the relay the phone uses. Souls Counted by each relay apart. The Souls page says whose count it shows; bug bounties are given on gogho.st. App updates, these docs, the website From gogho.st, as before. Not done yet: circles, spaces and calls across relays (the app uses one relay at a time, and an invite to a circle elsewhere says which relay to use first); who is online across relays; and signing in by username on another relay than the account's own, until a device that holds the account lists itself there. What it is One program on one port (8787 unless told otherwise), speaking plain HTTP and WebSockets. It has no dependencies beyond Dart's own library. You put a web server in front of it for TLS. Path What /hub (WebSocket) The hub: apps sign in with their key, find each other and pass sealed packets. It holds packets for people who are away (in memory, 96 MB at most), and keeps presence, rooms for circles, spaces and calls, usernames, sealed account backups and invite words. /relay/ channel (WebSocket) A phone and its paired computer when they're on different networks. /files/… Files spaces' sealed files, on disk. /word/ hash A circle's invite word. /link/… The pages a network sign-in comes back to, only with those networks set up. /market/… A Marketplace. The apps never read yours; the sample settings close it. /app/… The app in a browser, only where you give it a folder to serve. anything else Ghost Messaging relay as plain text: a quick check that it is up. It writes only under its data folder ( --data ): pairings, usernames, sealed account backups, Files, invites and invite words. Back that folder up if you care about any of it. Nothing it holds can be read without the apps' keys, but which installs talk to which is visible to whoever runs it, as with any server. What you need A server with a domain name pointed at it. Ports 80 and 443 open. A few hundred MB of memory. The source: github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging . Every sample file named on this page is in relay/deploy/ , and the image is built from relay/Dockerfile . The examples use relay.example.com . Put your own domain in its place. With Docker Compose This runs the relay with Caddy in front of it. Caddy gets and renews the certificate by itself once your domain's DNS points at the server. It needs Docker Compose 2.24 or later. cd relay/deploy cp relay.env.example relay.env # and edit: nothing in it is required cp Caddyfile.example Caddyfile # put your domain in place of relay.example.com docker compose up -d curl https://relay.example.com/ # Ghost Messaging relay The relay isn't published on any port of its own; only Caddy reaches it. What it keeps is in the relay-data volume. Compose pulls the relay's image, which every release publishes for x64 and arm64 machines: ghcr.io/infamousvague/ghost-relay , tagged with the version and latest . The image alone, without Compose: docker run -d --name ghost-relay --restart unless-stopped -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \ -v ghost-relay-data:/data --env-file relay.env ghcr.io/infamousvague/ghost-relay:latest To build it yourself instead, from the source's folder: docker build -t ghost-relay relay , and use ghost-relay in place of the published name. It runs as an unprivileged user, in an image with nothing but the program, the C library and certificates. Put a web server in front of it for TLS, as in the next section. As a single program, with systemd Each release publishes the program for Linux on x64 and arm64, with the service file beside it, on the releases page ( relay- and the version). Download the one for your machine, check it, and install it as a service: V=0.12.42 A=x64 # or arm64 curl -LO https://github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging/releases/download/relay-$V/ghost-relay-$V-linux-$A.tar.gz curl -LO https://github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging/releases/download/relay-$V/ghost-relay-$V-linux-$A.tar.gz.sha256 sha256sum -c ghost-relay-$V-linux-$A.tar.gz.sha256 tar xzf ghost-relay-$V-linux-$A.tar.gz cd ghost-relay-$V-linux-$A sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin ghost-relay sudo install -d -m 755 /opt/ghost-relay sudo install -m 755 ghost-relay /opt/ghost-relay/ghost-relay sudo install -d -o ghost-relay -g ghost-relay -m 700 /var/lib/ghost-relay sudo install -o root -g ghost-relay -m 640 relay.env /etc/ghost-relay.env sudo cp deploy/ghost-relay.service /etc/systemd/system/ sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now ghost-relay It listens on 127.0.0.1:8787 only, writes only to /var/lib/ghost-relay , and restarts if it stops. The settings file is optional: the service starts without one. To build the program yourself instead, with Dart 3.11 or later: dart compile exe bin/relay.dart -o ghost-relay in the source's relay folder. Then put a web server in front of it for TLS: Caddy: relay/deploy/Caddyfile.example , with relay:8787 changed to 127.0.0.1:8787 . nginx: relay/deploy/nginx.conf.example , with a certificate from certbot or similar. Whichever you use, it must pass WebSockets on, let a 10 MiB request body through (Files' pieces are up to 8 MiB), and not cut an open WebSocket off after a minute. Keep it on the same machine as the relay, so the relay sees each person's own address. The environment variables relay/deploy/relay.env.example lists every variable the relay reads, grouped by what each switches on. None is required: with no file at all it runs the hub, pairings, Files and invite words with their defaults. One NAME=value a line, no quotes, no spaces. Some values are secrets, so keep the filled-in copy where only root or the relay's own user can read it. The sample sets three things, and you should keep them: Variable What it is GHOST_PUBLIC_URL Your relay's https address, with no slash after. Its built-in default is not yours. GHOST_ADMIN_NAMES Set empty. Its built-in default is someone else's username. GHOST_MARKET_ON Set to 0 , which closes the relay's own Marketplace. The apps never read yours. The rest are optional: Variable What it switches on PORT The port, where --port isn't given (8787). --host and --data are options on the command line, not variables. GHOST_HUB_NAMES Every host name your relay is reached at, commas between. Sign-ins are then bound to the name the app dialled ( below ). GHOST_HUB_KEEP_HELD 1 keeps what is held for people who are away on the server's disk too, still sealed, so a restart doesn't lose it. GHOST_WIRE_MB , GHOST_WIRE_EACH_MB , GHOST_WIRE_STALL_S , GHOST_WIRE_IN_STALL_S How much every connection may hold together (64 MB), how much may wait for one (8 MB) and for how long (10 seconds going out, 20 coming in) before it is ended. The defaults suit a relay with 300 MB; give more where it has more. GHOST_TURN_SECRET , GHOST_TURN_URLS , GHOST_TURN_TTL Calls through your own TURN server . The secret and the addresses go together: both, or neither. GHOST_LINK_HELPERS Where your link helpers are: https addresses, commas between, 4 at most. Without it devices make direct links only on one network. GHOST_FED , GHOST_PUBLIC_HUB , GHOST_FED_ALLOW , GHOST_FED_BLOCK Talking to other relays : off (the default), open or list , your hub's own address, and the relays allowed or never linked with. GHOST_FED_PACKETS_A_MINUTE , GHOST_FED_BYTES_A_DAY , GHOST_FED_LOOKUPS_AN_HOUR What one linked relay may send yours. GHOST_FED_PORTS , GHOST_FED_PLAIN More ports other relays may be dialled at, and 1 to dial without TLS, which you want only between machines you run yourself. GHOST_FED_VIA , GHOST_FED_STANDING For a relay with no address of its own: the public relay it stays linked to. And, on a public relay, which such relays may stay linked to it. GHOST_FILES_… Files spaces' limits, each with a default. The defaults allow very large files: lower GHOST_FILES_TOTAL to fit your disk. GHOST_WEB_DIR , GHOST_APP_ORIGIN The app in a browser: a folder holding the browser build, served under /app/ (the same as --web ), or the address it is served from where that is one of its own. GHOST_TWILIO_SID , GHOST_TWILIO_TOKEN , GHOST_TWILIO_VERIFY , GHOST_TEXT_TO , GHOST_TEXTS_A_DAY Verifyin
